prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping and its realisation at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep optical lattice clocks (B006) as my single-part preferred configuration, with Katori and Ye. The chair's first question is whether this is a new invention or a further step in precision after the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes. My answer is that the magic-wavelength lattice is a new physical idea: it cancels the light shift of the clock transition so that thousands of atoms can be held Doppler- and recoil-free without perturbing the line, and this removed the old trade-off between atom number (stability) and perturbation (accuracy). The 2005 prize honoured the comb as a ruler and the 2012 prize honoured control of single trapped ions; neither contains this idea. The result has been reproduced and surpassed in several independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE), every systematic can be traced to a physical effect, and it has opened measurable regimes: gravitational redshift across a millimetre-scale sample, many-body clock physics, and searches for varying constants and dark matter. Credit is two names with a concept-and-realisation citation: Katori for the magic-wavelength concept and the first strontium lattice clocks, Ye for taking accuracy and stability to the record level. I do not propose a second part: no second shortlisted achievement is both mature and attributable within the one-person remaining room, and I do not want to add a part just because the limit allows it.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains overlap and attribution. Some colleagues will read this as an extraordinary refinement of a line already recognised twice, and a prize for a precision record invites the question of why Ludlow, Lemonde, Hinkley, Bloom and the Yb, Hg and Al+ clock communities are not named. I have not verified the 2001-03 priority record for the magic-wavelength idea and am relying on memory, so I support an expert report before the vote. The SI second has not been redefined and the fundamental-physics payoffs are still pending, so timing could be read as either ripe or early. I also accept that Katori and Ye may be weighted unequally, and that the citation must not read as a pure record.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B006 with Katori and Ye, names the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes as the main objection, and asks whether the citation should name the magic-wavelength concept and the 10^-18 realisation explicitly so that Yb, Al+ and other clock groups are not read as excluded.
responses.response: I agree with him on the wording, and I have changed my own citation to name the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 realisation rather than the precision record. Naming the concept makes it clear that the prize is for the invention and its demonstration, and leaves the comparison clocks (Yb, Al+, Hg) as validation and extension of the same standard rather than excluded rivals. Where I am cautious is his disclosure of a year in Hall's laboratory at JILA. I do not think it requires recusal as he reports no collaboration with Katori or Ye, but the chair should record it and I would not want the committee to rely on him alone for the priority question.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers topological insulators (B004) as a new symmetry-protected state of matter with a surprising theoretical prediction followed by a decisive HgTe experiment, and asks whether a new state of matter should take priority over a better ruler.
responses.response: I take the priority question seriously and B004 remains my first alternative; I agree the Z2 class is conceptually original. But I do not think novelty of a state of matter outranks a clean credit line. The credit boundary among Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang (Zhang deceased), Fu-Kane-Mele and Moore-Balents is still untidy, and the 2016 prize covers closely related conceptual ground, so a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize leaves visible gaps that I cannot repair within three names. If condensed-matter colleagues convinced me that the boundary is clean, I would reconsider, but nothing in round 1 has done that. I also note a ruler that opens new physics (redshift across a millimetre, many-body clock effects) is more than a better ruler.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers magic-angle graphene (B009) because a compact continuum model made a sharp prediction that experiment confirmed, and states that the pairing mechanism is unresolved but that the phenomena are reproduced.
responses.response: I share his taste for mechanism-first, controlled theory, and the Bistritzer-MacDonald to Jarillo-Herrero link is as striking a prediction-to-discovery story as the shortlist offers. My difficulty is that the field is about eight years old, the superconducting pairing is open, and the credit leaves Yuan Cao and other 2018 experimentalists and earlier twisted-bilayer theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto) outside the three names. Reproducibility of the phenomena is not in dispute, but I weigh maturity differently: I would revisit B009 in a few years when the mechanism is clearer. He himself calls B006 the most uncontested on maturity and reproducibility, which is the point on which we agree.

responses.point: Lindroth keeps B006 first, argues the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct concept, and admits she has not settled how to weigh Katori's idea against the performance records from Ye's group.
responses.response: I agree with her and share her unease. My answer is that the citation should rest on the invention and its realisation, so that the credit is shared by concept and demonstration, and I would ask for an expert report on the 2001-03 priority record before the vote rather than settle it by memory. We both rank B023 as a fallback, but I do not think it is ready: our own trios (Bloch, Greiner, Zoller) differ from Mehlig's (Bloch, Cirac, Zoller), which shows the allocation across five credited names is unsettled.

uncertainties: Whether an expert report on the 2001-03 magic-wavelength priority record would favour Katori's concept and, if so, how heavily it should weigh against the Ye-group performance records.
Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as a new invention distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes; I judge that it is, but others disagree.
Whether Ludlow, Lemonde, Hinkley or ion-clock leaders have claims that two names leave out, and whether concept-and-realisation wording is enough to answer them.
Whether condensed-matter colleagues could resolve the Kane-Mele versus BHZ credit boundary for B004 well enough for it to overtake clocks; I defer to them.
statement.conflict_note: I disclose a possible recusal issue on circuit QED (B015): as a circuit-QED theorist and director of WACQT I work closely with the Yale and ETH-linked community around Schoelkopf, Girvin, Blais and Wallraff. B015 is not in my configuration, and I will not argue for it. I have no personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or the other credited candidates in my configuration or alternatives (B004, B023). I also note the shared Gothenburg environment with Mehlig and Olsson reported in round 1. I do not consider these a reason to recuse from B006.
